newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader offers compromise over poll date.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader offers compromise over poll date.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, locked in a constitutional row with parliament, offered a compromise to his opponents after a large protest rally against him on Saturday.

But his move, offering to delay a controversial referendum on his powers, was by no means certain to defuse a bitter dispute with parliamentary deputies who accuse him of leading Belarus on the road to dictatorship.
Lukashenko addressed thousands of delegates at an "All-Belarus People's Congress" called to discuss his economic programme to 2000 and a referendum he had wanted to hold on November 7.
"I decided yesterday, and am asking for your agreement today, to hold the referendum on November 24," he said.
Lukashenko's opponents in parliament, which by the constitution must fix any referendum date, had twice voted to hold the poll on November 24.
"I declare here today, that I am ready for compromise today, right now, on grounds of principle, and not as a result of haggling with political extremists," Lukashenko said.
Lukashenko's referendum questions involve constitutional amendments which would extend his term, due to end in July 1999, by more than two years, and broaden his powers.
A referendum proposed by the deputies would ask the nation of 10 million to scrap the presidency altogether.
Thousands of people gathered in central Minsk earlier on Saturday to oppose Lukashenko's referendum. Riot police prevented them reaching the Palace of Sport where his congress was being held.
Lukashenko appeared to be falling in line with the existing constitution, under which only parliament can fix the date of a referendum called by the president.
The speech, broadcast on all three television channels, was followed by interviews with pro-Lukashenko deputies who said he had consulted them on Friday about the referendum date.
They praised him for his offer of compromise and said they would support him. The congress is due to continue on Sunday, when delegates are expected to approve Lukashenko's plan.

"If he has really decided to hold the referendum legally, then it is the beginning of stabilisation," Stanislav Shushkevich, head of the social democrat party and anti- Lukashenko deputy, told Reuters after the speech.
It was not immediately clear what effect Lukashenko's compromise would have on the deputies' proposed referendum.
